Ranking, resolve order, effort suggestion and clamping, and row selection exactly as in R-01..R-06 and A-01, including the max_rows edge cases and the order of gateway models before apps.
Result id format '<cid>|<model>|<effort>|<12-hex BLAKE2s-48>' with Python-identical hashes. Row title 'Name · Model', subtitle '<effort> effort · tags', meta description '“prompt” · subtitle'.
Default icons: system-search-symbolic, user-available-symbolic and emblem-system-symbolic. gicon is produced through gio::ThemedIcon to_string.

Gateway HTTP: GET <url>/model/info with an optional Bearer key read from secrets.env[key_env], 0.5 s timeout, 60 s cache, 30 s back-off, the model_info field semantics, and '<base>@<effort>' chat model ids.

Commands are spawned with no shell, stdin/stdout/stderr on /dev/null, cwd expanded with ~ and ~user, the inherited environment, and requires lookup over $PATH followed by ~/.local/bin and ~/bin. Optional argument groups are dropped when a placeholder in them is empty.
Clipboard: `wl-copy -- <text>`, falling back to `xclip -selection clipboard` on stdin.

Keyboard shortcut: the path /org/gnome/settings-daemon/plugins/media-keys/custom-keybindings/llm-search/, the relocatable custom-keybinding schema with the keys name, command and binding, command '<HOME>/.local/bin/llm-search prompt', and the path appended to the custom-keybindings list. Accelerator names come from gtk accelerator_name.
~/.config/environment.d/60-llm-search.conf (XDG_CONFIG_HOME is honored), with the identical comment and XDG_DATA_DIRS line, so existing installs print 'keeping'.

CLI verbs and options: install [--copy] [--dry-run] [--name|--category-name] [--shortcut], uninstall [--purge] [--dry-run], status, query WORDS, prompt|open [TEXT], test, help/-h/--help. Exit codes 0/1/2, warning: and error: prefixes, the usage text, the existing status lines, and query printing the raw reply tuple.
./install.sh forwards all install options.
Log prefix 'llm-search: ' and the lines 'running <argv0> in <cwd>' and 'opening <url before ?>'. Prompts are never logged.
Legacy cleanup of the io.github.oscillatingjem.LlmSearchProvider files and of the 0.1.0 .ini link.
Settings window wording for the existing rows, toasts ('Updated from agents.toml', 'Defaults restored', "Couldn't save: …", 'Key saved', 'Key removed'), and the documentation URLs.
contracts_changed: Runtime: Python 3.11+ and PyGObject are no longer needed. The binary needs the GTK ≥ 4.14, libadwaita ≥ 1.5 and glibc ≥ 2.39 shared libraries. The service Exec lines run `<bin> provider` and `<bin> app --gapplication-service`, and PYTHONPATH no longer leaks into launched agents. Migration: run ./install.sh once and log out and back in.

The program lives at $XDG_DATA_HOME/llm-search/bin/llm-search, an atomic copy. ~/.local/bin/llm-search now links to that copy instead of to a checkout. `--copy` is accepted but does nothing. `uninstall` without --purge now removes the binary (previously it left the --copy directory behind).

`llm-search test` now validates the config (it is an alias of the new `llm-search check`) instead of running the Python unit tests; developers use `cargo test`. The example agents.toml comment that suggests `python3 -c "import tomllib…"` now suggests `llm-search check`.

Stricter typing at load. enabled and copy_prompt must be booleans (the string "false" used to count as true). tags, models, efforts, requires and patterns must be arrays of strings (a bare string used to mean characters or substrings). command items must be strings or arrays of strings. min_chars, max_rows and low_effort_max_words must be integers (floats used to work). priority, weight and idle_minutes accept an integer or a float. App ids must match [A-Za-z0-9._-]+ and be unique. `check` and the installer print exactly which entries fail.

Validation moves to load time. Regex patterns, url/chat_url templates (only {prompt}, {model} and {effort} plus {{ }}; str.format specs, conversions and positional fields are gone) and alias targets are checked when the config loads, not on a particular search or activation.

Error handling. An invalid config no longer kills the provider or turns every search into a D-Bus error. Both processes keep the last good config, or start with no agents, and log the error; the prompt box shows a banner and the settings window a status page.

Regex engine: user patterns run on fancy-regex (case-insensitive) instead of Python re. They are compatible for the shipped patterns and for the usual syntax, including lookaround and backrefs. They differ for \< \>, \Z, $ before a final newline, {,n}, [[ inside classes, \N{…}, octal escapes, and some Unicode \w/\b/\s/case-folding cases. `check` lints for these, and the docs stop recommending the 'Python flavor'.

URL templates: placeholder values are still percent-encoded and query parameters left empty are still dropped (with the '?' removed when the query ends up empty). Literal template text is now left untouched: the documented folder=/home/you/... example stays readable instead of becoming %2F…, '+' is no longer turned into %20, key-only literal parameters such as '?flag' are kept, and schemes and '//' are no longer normalized.
requires absolutization: only argv items that come from literal template text are swapped for their which() path. A prompt or model that happens to equal 'claude' or 'ptyxis' is no longer rewritten.

Editor output: strings are written as readable UTF-8 instead of json \uXXXX escapes (so emoji values can now be saved). A missing key is appended at the end of its table instead of directly under the header. A symlinked agents.toml is written through to its target instead of being replaced, with an fsync before the rename. Restore Defaults writes idle_minutes = 30 (an integer, as the spin row does). Spin rows save 600 ms after the last change instead of on every step. Edits refuse to produce invalid configs (whole-config validation) rather than relying on readback.
secrets.env is written atomically (a 0600 temp file plus rename), the key keeps its line position, duplicates are dropped, and values containing a newline are refused.
The legacy 0.4.0 settings.toml migration runs during `llm-search install` instead of on every config load.

Launched commands get a new process group (process_group(0)) instead of a new session (setsid), and they are reaped explicitly. The prompt box opens URIs through gtk::UriLauncher, so the activation token is passed on.

Gateway: the first fetch happens immediately, which fixes the 60 s blind spot after boot. Every malformed JSON shape now yields [] instead of an error. In the prompt box and the settings Test button the fetch runs off the UI thread. HTTPS gateway URLs depend on open question 2: the recommended plain-HTTP build rejects https:// with a clear validation message.
Shortcut: setting the binding from the settings window keeps an existing custom name instead of forcing 'Agent Search'. Removing the shortcut no longer needs python3.

Installer: the environment.d safety check accepts /usr/share with or without the trailing slash. `prompt` no longer needs the gapplication binary. `query` quotes words correctly. `status` adds an environment.d line and a version line (both additive).
Process names in the docs and kill instructions change from `-m llm_search` to `llm-search provider` and `llm-search app`. The installer stops both generations.

The settings window now edits everything in agents.toml: add, delete and rename agents, all agent fields, aliases, rules and patterns, the gateway including key_env, and Restore Defaults. On disk it is still the same commented agents.toml.
risks_and_mitigations: Distro rustc is too old (Ubuntu 24.04 tops out at 1.91 and Debian 13 stable ships 1.85, while gtk-rs 0.11/0.22 needs 1.92). Mitigation: prebuilt binaries are the recommended path, and the docs name rustup for Ubuntu 24.04 and trixie-backports for Debian 13. Falling back to gtk4 0.10 is rejected because the line is outdated.

Raising a feature flag above v4_14/v1_5 by accident would make the binary fail at load on Ubuntu 24.04 or Debian 13 (BIND_NOW). Mitigation: pin the features in Cargo.toml, build releases only on pinned ubuntu-24.04 (whose system-deps would refuse newer APIs at build time), and stay away from ButtonRow, ToggleGroup and AdwShortcutLabel.

ubuntu-latest moves to 26.04 between Oct and Nov 2026, which would silently raise the runtime minimums. Mitigation: `runs-on: ubuntu-24.04` everywhere, plus a CI check that `ldd` and objdump report no glibc symbol above 2.39.

Regex semantics drift in users' own patterns. Mitigation: compile at load, lint for the known divergent constructs, test the shipped patterns against the Python match matrix, have the installer print warnings on upgrade, and document the changes. fancy-regex's backtrack limit bounds pathological patterns.

toml_edit decor surprises: a multi-line array collapsed by fmt(), comments that belong to the next header's prefix, CRLF handling. Mitigation: never call fmt() on user arrays, copy decor explicitly, and rely on the edit-and-revert identity tests and per-operation golden files. Whatever toml_edit does with CRLF is documented once and tested.

TOML 1.1 versus Python tomllib during rollback: the Rust parser accepts 1.1 syntax that Python 0.5 rejects. Mitigation: the editor only emits TOML 1.0 constructs, and until 1.0 CI runs python3 tomllib on the golden outputs.

The cutover could leave old processes holding the bus names (a 60 s provider, a box resident up to idle_minutes). Mitigation: the installer stops both generations; status shows whether each is running.

Registering the D-Bus object too late would drop calls from an activated start. Mitigation: register in ApplicationImpl::dbus_register (a subclass), never override local_command_line, never set IS_SERVICE on the prompt box, and cover activation-time calls with the TestDBus tests.

Blocking work on the main loop: the gateway fetch and regex evaluation run inside D-Bus and GTK handlers. Mitigation: ureq's global 0.5 s timeout bounds the provider fetch (DNS included); the prompt box and the settings window use gio::spawn_blocking; patterns are precompiled once per load.

A panic in a GTK callback aborts the process (PyGObject only printed the error). Mitigation: every launch, save, regex and gateway path returns Result and surfaces it as a toast, a banner or a D-Bus error. Clippy forbids unwrap in non-test code (clippy::unwrap_used), with panic=unwind left as the default.

Scope creep in the full editor (Phase 3 is the least predictable). Mitigation: one generic StringListGroup and a single instant-apply save path. Reordering, drag and drop, and per-field undo are out of scope for 1.0, and the 7-11 day estimate has an explicit cut line: reorder of rules and the alias target suggestion list can slip to 1.1.

gtk-rs churn: 0.11.x patch releases have added and reverted APIs, and 0.12/0.23 is probably due around GNOME 52. Mitigation: commit Cargo.lock, use --locked builds, run an MSRV job, and plan one upgrade pass about every 6-12 months.
Only the owner's GNOME 50 machine gets real-session testing. Mitigation: smoke tests in distro containers plus clear 'tested on' labels in the README; ask early users on other distros to report.

Unverified facts to check on day one of Phase 1, once the toolchain is installed: regex/fancy-regex handling of {,n}, İ/ı and U+001C; the default table decor in toml_edit; ureq's timeout_global covering DNS; libadwaita NavigationView and Banner needing no flag above v1_5 (believed 1.4 and 1.3).
open_questions_for_owner: Version scheme: 0.9.0 for the dogfood/beta builds and 1.0.0 for the public Rust release, or carry on with 0.6.0?

HTTPS gateways: plain-HTTP-only ureq (fewest dependencies; localhost LiteLLM works; https:// rejected with a clear message), or turn on ureq's rustls feature (about 20-30 more crates, roughly +1-2 MB) so remote https gateways keep working as they do today?
Is appending missing keys at the end of their table (toml_edit's default, which reads more naturally) acceptable, or should placement directly under the header and id line be kept with extra code?
Should the ranker keep exact bug parity for max_rows <= 1 (an explicit @gateway row replaced by the best app), as this plan does, or should that be fixed in 1.0?

Branching: develop on a long-lived `rust` branch and merge to main at Phase 3, or merge each phase to main once it is green? When should each push happen? (The plan assumes an explicit approval for every push and every tag.)
Is dropping float values for min_chars, max_rows and low_effort_max_words, and string booleans, acceptable as a 1.0 break, given that `check` and the installer report them?
Publish aarch64 prebuilt binaries as well (an ubuntu-24.04-arm runner), or x86_64 only for 1.0?
Keep the 0.4.0 settings.toml migration at all (it now runs in install), or drop it and document the manual step for anyone upgrading straight from 0.4?
After 1.0, keep tests/parity/gen_vectors.py in the repo as a historical record, or delete it and keep only the generated JSON fixtures?

Is packaging beyond the tarball wanted later (a Fedora COPR, an AUR PKGBUILD)? If so, the dependency versions should be kept installable from Fedora's packaged rust-* crates (for example, Fedora packages fancy-regex 0.16 rather than 0.19).

judgements.lens: CORRECTNESS AND SAFETY: does the plan provably preserve behavior and contracts (parity harness quality, regex semantics, TOML comment preservation, D-Bus contract, config migration), and can each phase be rolled back without data loss?

scores.plan: Plan 1: RISK-FIRST (oracle + differential harness, per-component cutover, schema freeze)
scores.strengths: Has the strongest parity proof of the three. (1) It runs an executable Python oracle (a JSONL op server with python3 -I and monkeypatched seams), uses about 20k committed goldens, and runs a live differential with fresh seeds (200k cases per change, 1M before exit). (2) It checks every code point (0x110000) against Python for split, strip, capitalize, lower and the regex \w, \s, \d and \b probes, using tables generated from Python 3.14. (3) Every deviation goes in deviations.toml, keyed by spec ID and classified A (match exactly), B (deliberate change) or C (bug kept for now). Bug fixes never ship in the same release as a cutover. (4) The editor is compared byte for byte with Python over mutated and pathological files: CRLF, quoted keys, fake headers inside strings, U+2028. Today's below-header key placement and decor rules are reproduced (T-04..T-10). (5) A cross-readability gate requires every Rust-written file to parse with tomllib, load with config.load, and give the same values as the Rust loader. Together with a schema freeze and TOML 1.0-only output, this keeps rollback to Python free of data loss. (6) Before switching, a preflight runs the user's own agents.toml through the oracle and through Rust. (7) A Phase 0 spike proves the rollback mechanism first: swap the Exec line, call ReloadConfig, and confirm no logout is needed. The last two binary versions are kept in state/bin. (8) Core returns an Action enum, so activations can be compared with no side effects. (9) The D-Bus replay diff covers the error names, the idle exit and LaunchSearch. The D-Bus object is registered in dbus_register, each call holds the app, and catch_unwind sits at handler boundaries. (10) Python 'unanchored $' is translated to (?=\n?\z) and \Z to \z, and the remaining İ/ı difference is documented.
scores.weaknesses: (1) It misreads the first-60-s gateway quirk. The plan emulates it 'by starting the clock at process start', but Python's time.monotonic counts from boot, not from process start. The provider exits after 60 s idle, so a fresh provider would skip the fetch for its whole life and gateway rows would effectively vanish from GNOME search. This must be corrected: use CLOCK_MONOTONIC (glib::monotonic_time) for exact parity, or fix it deliberately with Option<Instant> as a class B change. (2) It says soup3 gives a '0.5 s timeout as today', but soup Session timeouts are whole seconds, so a Cancellable plus a glib timeout is needed. (3) The regex translator (rewriting \w and \b with lookaround, rewriting \s inside classes) is itself a large source of bugs, although the exhaustive probes help. (4) It is very large, about 16-21 weeks, and soak gates depend on one person's discipline. (5) The async reply to GetInitialResultSet needs care so that stored rows are swapped only when the reply is sent. The plan states this but does not test interleaving.

scores.plan: Plan 2: USER-CONTINUITY-FIRST (prompt box first, short hybrid, delete Python in Phase 2)
scores.strengths: (1) Goldens are exported from a frozen v0.5.0 and cover every spec ID family, plus per-code-point tables, a pyre audit of the owner's real patterns, and a DIVERGENCES.toml allowlist limited to a fixed policy. (2) The TestDBus provider suite is first validated against the Python provider and then has to pass unchanged against Rust, which proves the harness itself. (3) The installer golden is captured from a real bash run in a container. A real v0.5.0 install is upgraded in a container. The Rust installer deliberately keeps the same symlinks, so the old bash installer can take them back (rollback without hitting 'exists and is not a symlink'). (4) Through Phase 3, CI runs tomllib and llm_search.config.load on every file the editor writes. With the schema freeze, this keeps v0.5.0 rollback viable. (5) Below-header key placement and decor copying are kept. Phase 3 adds edit-and-inverse byte-identity tests. Array::fmt() is never called on existing arrays. (6) soup3 with a Cancellable enforces the sub-second timeout correctly and also bounds DNS. (7) A separate gio-only CLI binary means the installer still runs, and prints hints, when libadwaita is missing (BIND_NOW). (8) In Phase 4 each fix is its own commit that changes one golden case.
scores.weaknesses: (1) It contradicts itself. It declares Phases 1-2 strict parity, but Phase 1 changes behavior: a lenient loader (unknown keys become warnings, a string becomes a list, invalid entries are skipped), invalid regexes are disabled instead of failing, URL templates are cut down to {name} and {{ }} only, and the gateway fetches in the first 60 s. These land in the only hybrid window, where the Rust box and the Python provider read the same config, so the two can disagree. (2) The ranking differential is weak: a 500-prompt corpus through D-Bus, with no live seeded fuzzing and no edit differential against Python's bytes. (3) Several writer changes (UTF-8, CRLF kept, numeric type following the existing value) are allowlisted up front instead of proven at parity first. (4) Once Phase 2 deletes Python, the only route back is checking out the v0.5.0 tag; there is no per-component rollback. (5) Rollback is rehearsed only once per phase.

scores.plan: Plan 3: SIMPLEST-ARCHITECTURE (one binary, big-bang cutover, deliberate behavior changes)
scores.strengths: (1) Before any write, save() runs a full load() and validate() on the serialized result and refuses to write if it fails. The write is atomic, keeps symlinks and fsyncs. (2) It has edit-and-revert identity tests and per-operation golden files. (3) A TestDBus test asserts that an invalid edit keeps the old rows, and ActivateResult is tested with a real 'touch' command. (4) Regexes are compiled once at load, with a lint for constructs that differ from Python, and the shipped patterns are tested against Python's match matrix. (5) The blake2s-48 vectors are kept exactly. (6) CI checks that the binary needs no glibc symbol above 2.39 and pins ubuntu-24.04. (7) Until 1.0, CI runs tomllib on the golden outputs. (8) It keeps both bus names, so the D-Bus contract is unchanged byte for byte.
scores.weaknesses: (1) Parity cannot be proven. There is no oracle and no differential harness, only one-off vectors. The Python-derived tests are rewritten to match the new contract, which weakens the reference itself. Many behavior changes ship in the same cutover. (2) Loading becomes stricter: float min_chars and max_rows are rejected, and so are string booleans and string-for-list values. Configs that load today fail, and the provider then starts with no agents. (3) Missing keys move to the end of the table, the toml_edit default. The spec flags placement as observable. (4) URL template normalization, requires absolutization, the capitalize behavior for non-ASCII, setsid replaced by process_group, and the timing of the legacy migration all change at once. (5) The plain-HTTP ureq default rejects https gateways that work today. (6) It accepts that CRLF behavior is 'whatever toml_edit preserves'. (7) There is no regex translator, only a lint, so the semantics of $, \Z and \< and the Unicode classes differ silently for patterns the lint misses. (8) Rollback covers the whole app: uninstall, check out v0.5.0, reinstall and log out. There is no per-component switch.

best_ideas_to_graft: From Plan 1: an executable Python oracle (a JSONL op server run with python3 -I, side-effect seams monkeypatched) paired with a Rust parity binary that speaks the same protocol, giving golden replay in CI plus live seeded differential runs (for example, 1M cases before each exit) with zero unexplained diffs.
From Plan 1: a deviations allowlist keyed by parity-spec ID, with classes A (match), B (deliberate) and C (bug kept, fixed later). No bug fix ships in the same release as an engine cutover.

From Plan 1: a cross-readability gate. Every file the Rust writer produces, scalar or structural, must parse with tomllib, load with config.load, and give the same values as the Rust loader. Combine it with a schema freeze and TOML-1.0-only output until Python is retired.

From Plan 1: a byte-for-byte edit differential against Python over mutated and pathological configs (CRLF, quoted and dotted keys, fake headers inside multi-line strings, U+2028, multi-line arrays), with today's below-header or below-id-line placement for missing keys.

From Plan 1: exhaustive per-code-point checks against Python for split, strip, splitlines, capitalize and lower, and single-character regex class probes for \w, \s, \d and \b, with the tables generated by a checked-in Python script.
From Plan 1: a preflight that runs the user's own agents.toml (patterns, aliases, agents) through the oracle and through Rust, and refuses the engine switch on any difference.

From Plan 1: a Phase 0 spike proving rollback by Exec swap plus org.freedesktop.DBus.ReloadConfig, with no logout, on dbus-broker. Keep the last two binary versions so rollback is possible within Rust as well.
From Plan 1: core returns an Action enum (Copy, Spawn, OpenUri, Nothing), so activation parity can be compared without running anything.
From Plan 2: run the TestDBus SearchProvider2 suite against the Python provider first to validate the harness, then require it to pass unchanged against Rust.

From Plan 2: capture an installer golden from a real bash install in a container, and test an upgrade from a real v0.5.0 install. The Rust installer keeps the same symlink targets as symlinks, so the old bash installer can take them back on rollback.
From Plan 2: enforce the 0.5 s gateway timeout with a gio::Cancellable plus a glib timeout, because soup3 Session timeouts are whole seconds. This also bounds DNS.
From Plan 2: a gio-only CLI and installer binary, so that install and status run and can print dependency hints even when libadwaita fails to load (BIND_NOW).
From Plan 2: a pyre audit of the owner's real routing patterns against Python re over a prompt corpus, committed as a golden.

From Plan 3: a whole-config load() and validate() on the serialized result before any write, refusing the write on any error, plus edit-and-inverse byte-identity tests and a D-Bus test showing that an invalid on-disk edit keeps the last good rows.
From Plan 3: a CI check (ldd or objdump) that the release binary references no glibc symbol above the 2.39 baseline, in addition to pinning ubuntu-24.04.

Correction for the final plan: reproduce the gateway cache start exactly, with time measured from boot (CLOCK_MONOTONIC via glib::monotonic_time) and fetched/failed starting at 0. Alternatively, fix it deliberately with Option<Instant> as an allowlisted change. Never start the clock at process start.
fatal_flaws: Plan 1: it emulates the 'no fetch in the first 60 s after boot' quirk by starting the clock at process start. Python's time.monotonic counts from boot, and the provider exits after 60 s idle, so every freshly activated Rust provider would skip the gateway fetch for its whole life. Gateway rows would effectively disappear from GNOME search, which breaks the very parity the plan claims. This is fixable but must be corrected before adoption.

Plan 2: it claims strict parity for Phases 1-2, but Phase 1 already ships behavior changes: a lenient loader that warns on unknown keys, coerces a string to a list and skips invalid entries; disabled invalid regexes; URL templates restricted to {name} and {{ }}; an early gateway fetch. These land in the only hybrid window, where the Rust prompt box and the Python search provider read the same config, so the two can show different rows or errors. That breaks the plan's own rule that fixes wait until Python is gone.

Plan 3: its correctness rests on rewritten tests and one-off vectors, with no oracle or differential harness. The cutover bundles many behavior changes, including stricter typing that makes previously valid configs (float min_chars, string booleans, a string where a list is expected) fail to load, leaving no agents. Regressions therefore cannot be told apart from intended changes, and parity cannot be proven.

Plan 3: the plain-HTTP ureq default rejects https:// gateway URLs that work today through urllib, a silent contract regression unless the owner opts into rustls. Missing keys also move to the end of their table, which the spec flags as an observable editor contract.

No plan relies on an API that the verified facts say does not exist. All three correctly use pre_exec with setsid or process_group (std's setsid is nightly-only), register the D-Bus object in dbus_register, and avoid IS_SERVICE and local_command_line overrides on the prompt box.

judgements.lens: FEASIBILITY AND EFFORT: whether the crate and API choices exist per the verified facts, whether the phases fit one AI-assisted maintainer, whether the estimates are honest, and whether anything missing would block a phase.

scores.plan: Plan 1: RISK-FIRST (oracle + differential harness, per-component cutover with engine switch)
scores.strengths: Every crate and API it relies on exists per the verified facts. These include gtk4 0.11.5 with v4_14, libadwaita 0.9.2 with v1_5, register_object inside dbus_register, raw method_call, hold guards, pre_exec(setsid) instead of the nightly-only setsid, soup3 0.9.0 with libsoup3-devel listed, Blake2sVar output size 6, fancy-regex RegexBuilder with case_insensitive and backtrack_limit, gio::TestDBus, and #[gtk::test] under xvfb with GSK_RENDERER=cairo. The provider crate links only gio, which keeps cold start low. Phase 0 includes a spike on Fedora 44 dbus-broker to prove that swapping the Exec line and calling ReloadConfig works without a logout. The rollback design depends on that assumption, so testing it first is correct. The Action enum ({Copy, Spawn, OpenUri, Nothing}) keeps the core pure and easy to compare. The estimates are honest: the plan itself says 16-21 weeks before soaks. The TOML-1.0 cross-readability gate and the schema freeze address a real hazard: tomllib rejects TOML 1.1 while the Rust parser accepts it.
scores.weaknesses: This is far more process than one maintainer needs. It calls for a JSONL oracle server and a parity binary, about 20k goldens plus 1M live differential cases, exhaustive Unicode probes over all 0x110000 code points, a shadow .Devel provider, a --compare mode, engine selection in the bash installer across 4 engine combinations, versioned binaries in state/bin, and four soaks of 7 days to 4 weeks. Total calendar time is roughly 5-7 months. The settings window gets built twice: a full parity port in Phase 4 (SW-01..25), then a rewrite in Phase 5. The regex translator rewrites \w and \b as Python-isalnum classes with lookaround, which sends every shipped pattern containing \b down fancy-regex's backtracking path and makes a large, fragile translator. The bash installer is kept but gains engine.conf, rollback and dual-generation logic, so the most fragile code grows. Phase 0 packs an oracle, a corpus generator, about 45 new Python tests, the spike, benchmarks and doc fixes into 5-7 days, which is tight.

scores.plan: Plan 2: USER-CONTINUITY-FIRST (Rust prompt box first in a short hybrid, then provider and CLI, then editor)
scores.strengths: The crate and API choices hold up against the verified facts. The provider is a gio::Application registered in dbus_register using typed_method_call(...).invoke_and_return_future_local. The hold guard is held per call. soup3 timeouts are whole seconds, so the 0.5 s limit is enforced with a Cancellable plus a glib timeout, which also covers DNS. Blake2sVar(6), fancy-regex with backtrack_limit, pre_exec(setsid), and Variant::print for query output are all real. Splitting the crates is a good feasibility call. The `llm-search` CLI and provider link only glib, gio and soup3, so install and check still run, and can print hints, on a machine without libadwaita. A GTK-linked binary would fail at load there because of BIND_NOW. Only Phase 1 is a hybrid, Python is frozen at that point, and Python is deleted in Phase 2, so the time spent maintaining two engines is short. The TestDBus harness is validated against the Python provider before it is used on Rust. The estimates are honest and broken down (46-71 focused days, with part-time doubling stated). The install.sh bootstrap checks cargo and the gtk4, libadwaita-1 and libsoup-3.0 pkg-config modules before building, which would otherwise block users. The Phase 0 pyre audit of the owner's real patterns is a good preflight.
scores.weaknesses: Phase 1 is overloaded: the full core, the prompt box, and full settings parity (SW-01..25 plus the shortcut dialog) in 14-20 days. The UI share of 5-7 days is optimistic. Like Plan 1, it ports the old settings window and then rebuilds it in Phase 3. Its own rule is that fixes wait for Phase 4, yet Phase 1 ships many divergences: lenient loading, disabled regexes instead of failed searches, {name}-only URL templates, UTF-8 and CRLF writes, numeric-type preservation, and symlink write-through. During the hybrid this makes the Rust prompt box and the Python GNOME search disagree on the same config. A pattern that fails to compile disables quietly in Rust but fails the Python search. Phase 2 rewrites the whole bash installer in Rust with exact message parity, plus the provider, in 9-13 days, which is aggressive. Some Tumbleweed package names are unverified.

scores.plan: Plan 3: SIMPLEST-ARCHITECTURE (one package, one binary, no old settings port, straight to the new editor)
scores.strengths: It has the smallest scope and the fewest dependencies: gtk4, adw, toml, toml_edit, serde, serde_json, fancy-regex, blake2 and ureq. There is no workspace, meson, async runtime, zbus, clap or libc. It never ports the old settings window, and the owner lives with 'Open agents.toml' during dogfooding, which removes the biggest duplicate effort in Plans 1 and 2. The widgets it uses are all within v1_5: SwitchRow 1.4, Banner 1.3, NavigationView 1.4, AlertDialog and Dialog 1.5, and it avoids ButtonRow (1.6) and AdwShortcutLabel (1.8). glib::shell_parse_argv and shell_quote, gtk::UriLauncher (v4_10), process_group(0), and gio::spawn_blocking with spawn_local are all real. A GTK-free lib enforced by a CI grep keeps `cargo test` independent of a display. It lists the facts to verify on day one ({,n}, İ, U+001C, toml_edit default decor, ureq DNS timeout), which is honest about the gaps. Its parity vectors are a single one-off script instead of a harness.
scores.weaknesses: The estimates look optimistic. The plan says 22-33 focused days in total. That includes a 5-7 day core (Unicode helpers, serde leniency, decor-preserving edits, migration, regex lint, a check command). It also includes a 6-9 day Phase 2 covering the provider, the prompt box, and a Rust installer with exact bash message parity plus D-Bus and install tests. Plan 2 budgets about 1.5-2x more for comparable work. A realistic figure is about 35-50 days. Because there is one binary, the provider mode and the CLI link GTK and libadwaita. Provider cold start pays the dynamic-load cost, and a prebuilt `llm-search install` on a machine missing libadwaita fails with a loader error before it can print the distro hint. Plain-HTTP ureq would regress https gateways that work today unless rustls is enabled, which the plan leaves as an open question. Most behavior changes land together in 1.0 (stricter types, a new URL template rule, requires absolutization, key placement, regex), so the Python vectors only check a subset. Regressions caused by these changes will not show up as clean parity diffs.

best_ideas_to_graft: From Plan 3: do not port the current 3-page settings window. Dogfood with 'preferences' opening agents.toml, then build the full editor once on toml_edit. This saves about 5-10 days that Plans 1 and 2 spend on a throwaway port.

From Plan 2: put the CLI and installer, and the provider mode, in a binary that links only glib, gio and soup3, never GTK or libadwaita. Then install, status and check run, and print distro hints, on machines missing libadwaita, and provider cold start avoids loading GTK. The GTK UI goes in a second binary.

From Plan 3: keep one GTK-free core library enforced by a CI grep, keep the dependency list minimal (hand-written quote(), process_group(0) or pre_exec), and keep a day-one checklist that verifies the unverified Rust facts ({,n}, İ/ı, U+001C, toml_edit default decor, the ureq/soup timeout covering DNS) once the toolchain is installed.

From Plan 1: add a Phase 0 spike proving that swapping the rendered .service Exec plus org.freedesktop.DBus.ReloadConfig plus a kill switches implementations without a logout on Fedora 44 dbus-broker, before relying on it for rollback.

From Plan 1: have activation in the core return an Action/LaunchPlan enum ({Copy, Spawn{argv,cwd}, OpenUri, Nothing}), with separate executors, so activation decisions can be golden-tested without spawning anything.

From Plans 1 and 2: until Python is deleted, run a cross-readability gate in CI that parses every Rust editor output with Python tomllib and config.load, and allow only TOML 1.0 output with no new schema keys. Rollback to v0.5.0 depends on this.
From Plan 2: build one TestDBus SearchProvider2 harness from generated .service files, validate it against the Python provider first, then require the Rust provider to pass it unchanged.

From Plan 2 (pyre audit) and Plan 1 (preflight): run the owner's real routing patterns through Python re and the fancy-regex translator over a prompt corpus before cutover, and report any construct whose meaning changes.

From Plan 2: the install.sh bootstrap checks cargo >= 1.92 and the pkg-config modules gtk4 >= 4.14, libadwaita-1 >= 1.5 and libsoup-3.0, and prints the per-distro command (backports or rustup for Debian 13 and Ubuntu 24.04) before attempting `cargo build --locked`.

From Plan 2: `llm-search prompt` calls ActivateAction or Activate directly with platform-data built from XDG_ACTIVATION_TOKEN and DESKTOP_STARTUP_ID, which drops the dependency on the gapplication binary while keeping focus behavior.

From Plan 2: soup3 with a Cancellable plus a glib timeout for the 0.5 s bound, because Session timeouts are whole seconds. This keeps https gateways working through glib-networking. Use ureq without TLS only if the owner confirms the gateway is plain-HTTP localhost.

From all plans: build releases on a pinned runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 with v4_14 and v1_5, run a container smoke matrix (Fedora 43/44, Debian 13, Ubuntu 24.04/26.04, Arch, Tumbleweed) that runs --version to catch BIND_NOW symbol failures, and run an MSRV 1.92 CI job.
fatal_flaws: Plan 1 (Phase 3): it emulates the Python 'no gateway fetch in the first 60 s after boot' quirk by starting the clock at process start. The provider exits after 60 s idle, so every provider process would skip the fetch for most or all of its life, and gateway model rows would effectively never appear. This is a serious regression, not parity. It is easy to fix (use Option<Instant>, or skip the emulation), but as written the 0.6.0 provider ships with broken gateway rows.

Plan 1 (overall): no API is missing, but the effort is close to fatal for one maintainer. The work is 16-21 working weeks plus 4 soak periods, including a 1M-case differential harness, exhaustive code-point probes, a .Devel shadow provider, a 4-way engine matrix in bash, and a settings window built twice. The plan risks stalling before Python is retired. Phase 7 needs at least 4 weeks on 0.9 before deletion.

Plan 3: no fatal API flaws. One conditional blocker: if the owner uses or wants https gateways, the plain-HTTP ureq build rejects URLs that work today, and the plan defers this to an open question. Decide it in Phase 0, either ureq with rustls or soup3.

Plan 2: no fatal API flaws. Phase 1 ships a hybrid in which the Rust prompt box and the frozen Python provider handle invalid regexes, unknown keys and URL templates differently, despite the stated strict-parity rule. Either hold those divergences until Phase 2 or accept and document the disagreement.

judgements.lens: END-STATE QUALITY: is the resulting architecture simple, idiomatic gtk-rs/libadwaita, easy to install on Fedora/Debian/Ubuntu/Arch/openSUSE/Silverblue (from source and prebuilt), easy to extend (full settings editor, gateway), and well tested?

scores.plan: Plan 1: RISK-FIRST (core/provider/app/parity workspace, bash installer kept, engine switching)
scores.strengths: Its testing is the strongest of the three: frozen goldens, a live Python/Rust differential harness, exhaustive per-code-point Unicode checks, a D-Bus replay diff, gio::TestDBus, #[gtk::test] under xvfb, and cross-readability gates. The D-Bus approach is idiomatic: one GApplication connection, register_object in dbus_register, a hold guard per call, and the reused INTERFACE_XML. The provider binary is gio-only, so it stays light. Core is pure, and activation returns an Action enum that tests can inspect without running anything. soup3 keeps https gateways and GNOME proxy settings working. Release binaries are built on a pinned ubuntu-24.04 runner with v4_14/v1_5. The full editor comes with structural ops, push_formatted decor handling, and a validator shared with --check-config.
scores.weaknesses: The end state is the most complex of the three. It keeps two languages for deployment: bash glue that shells out to `agent-search --remove-shortcut` and similar helpers. It ships four crates, including a parity crate. Binaries sit in versioned directories under ~/.llm-search/state/bin/<ver>-<sha>, which is unusual. Engine-selection scaffolding (engine.conf, --provider/--prompt, rollback) lasts until 1.0. The pyregex translator rewrites \w, \W and \b into Python-isalnum classes with lookaround. That forces every \b pattern onto fancy-regex's backtracking path, and it is fragile code to keep forever. The pycompat Unicode tables are generated by a Python script, so Python stays a dev dependency after Python is retired. Below-header key placement needs extra reordering code. The schema freeze lasts through Phase 7, which makes the editor harder to extend. Python remains the reference until the very end, so the end state arrives slowest (16-21 weeks plus soaks). Silverblue gets only a toolbox note.

scores.plan: Plan 2: USER-CONTINUITY-FIRST (core + GTK-free cli/provider binary + adw ui binary, Rust installer)
scores.strengths: The binary split is well chosen. `llm-search`, which hosts the CLI, the installer and the `search-provider` mode, links only glib/gio/soup3. That means the installer still runs on a machine missing libadwaita, where a GTK-linked binary would fail under BIND_NOW, and can print distro hints there. The provider also starts without loading GTK. The UI binary is a separate adw::Application. Bash is reduced to a thin install.sh bootstrap: use prebuilt binaries if present, otherwise check cargo>=1.92 and the pkg-config modules, then build with --locked. The shortcut code uses gio::Settings, which removes the python3 dependency. The provider uses typed_method_call with invoke_and_return_future_local, so the gateway fetch is async with a Cancellable timeout that also covers DNS. Loading is diagnostics-based and keeps the last good config, and `llm-search check` reports file:line positions. Binaries are copied atomically into $XDG_DATA_HOME/llm-search/bin while the symlinks stay, so a bash v0.5.0 rollback still works. The full editor has NavigationView subpages, whole-config validation, a reload/keep-mine banner, a schema-coverage test and inverse-op identity tests. Testing is strong: a TestDBus harness that is first validated against Python, installer snapshot and upgrade tests in containers, a smoke matrix on 7 distro images, and fuzzing. Distro instructions cover all targets, including Silverblue via toolbox.
scores.weaknesses: It has three crates and two binaries plus the bootstrap, which is reasonable but not minimal. The lenient-coercion layer (string-to-list, truthiness warnings, NaN->0) adds permanent code and keeps ambiguous configs alive instead of enforcing a clean schema. Keeping below-header placement needs extra code that fights toml_edit's defaults. soup3 adds libsoup3-devel as a build dependency, and its whole-second timeouts need a workaround. The internal 'quit' action is exposed on the session bus. Some openSUSE package names are unverified. The old settings window is ported at strict parity and then largely rebuilt in Phase 3, so some work is thrown away.

scores.plan: Plan 3: SIMPLEST-ARCHITECTURE (one package, one binary with provider/app/CLI modes, GTK-free lib target)
scores.strengths: It is the simplest and most idiomatic end state. There is one Cargo package with a GTK-free lib target, enforced by a CI grep, and no workspace, meson, build.rs, clap, async runtime or zbus. Templates are embedded with include_str!. The dependency list is short and pinned. The old settings window is not ported; the new editor is built directly on toml_edit with reusable widgets (StringListGroup, debounced SpinRow) and a single path for instant-apply saves. Validation is typed and errors are path-addressed. URL templating is simplified to {name}/{{ }}, and literal template text is no longer re-normalized, which removes a lot of urllib-emulation code. Missing keys are appended at the end of the table, as toml_edit does by default, which needs less code. Regex divergences are linted rather than emulated. Testing is solid: the 35 tests ported, parity vectors, TestDBus provider tests, installer tests with GSETTINGS_BACKEND=memory, edit-and-revert identity tests, and #[gtk::test]. CI runs on pinned ubuntu-24.04 with an MSRV job and an ldd/objdump glibc-symbol check, and releases are drafts. It is the fastest route to the end state (about 22-33 days).
scores.weaknesses: With a single GTK-linked binary, provider mode still maps and BIND_NOW-resolves libgtk/libadwaita on every overview search activation, so its cold start is worse than a gio-only provider. On a machine missing libadwaita, the prebuilt `./llm-search install` dies with a loader error instead of a hint. The plain-HTTP ureq default rejects https gateways that work today, which is a regression unless the rustls feature is enabled. Stricter typing breaks configs that load today: float min_chars, string booleans. Removing the --copy semantics is minor. Silverblue is not addressed explicitly. The README minimums are inconsistent (Fedora 40+ in Phase 0, Fedora 42+ in Phase 4). The Phase 2 'Open agents.toml' fallback leaves a period with no settings UI. Smoke testing on other distros goes only as far as `check` and `--dry-run`, without a TestDBus run.

best_ideas_to_graft: Split the binaries the way Plan 2 does. A GTK-free `llm-search` binary (glib/gio plus HTTP only) hosts the CLI, the installer and the search-provider mode, so the installer can diagnose missing GTK/libadwaita libraries and the provider never loads GTK. A separate adw `agent-search` binary hosts the prompt box and settings. Keep a single GTK-free core lib target, enforced in CI (Plan 3).

Replace the bash CLI and installer with Rust, using gio::Settings for the shortcut. Keep only a tiny install.sh bootstrap: prefer the prebuilt binaries, otherwise check cargo>=1.92 and the pkg-config modules, print per-distro hints, and run `cargo build --release --locked`.
Copy binaries atomically into $XDG_DATA_HOME/llm-search/bin and keep ~/.local/bin/llm-search and the other five targets as symlinks, so the v0.5.0 bash installer can still roll back cleanly.
Make activation pure. Core returns a LaunchPlan/Action enum {Copy, Spawn{argv,cwd}, OpenUri}, executors stay thin, and child processes are reaped with glib child_watch or a waiter thread.

Validate at load time with path-addressed diagnostics, a `llm-search check` command (keep `test` as an alias), and last-good-config retention in both processes. Compile regexes once at load, disable bad patterns with a report, and use fancy-regex backtrack_limit.
Lint Python-divergent regex constructs instead of emulating Python's \w and \b with lookaround (Plan 3 over Plan 1). Translate only the cheap cases: \Z to \z, {,n} to {0,n}, and \< / \> to literals.
Simplify URL templating to {prompt}/{model}/{effort} plus {{ }}, and stop re-normalizing literal template query text (Plan 3).

Use a single ConfigDoc over toml_edit with typed structural ops. Gate every save with whole-config validation, then an atomic write through the symlink target with fsync and the old file's mode. Test with edit-and-inverse identity tests, a schema-coverage test that lists every agents.toml key, and per-op golden files.

Build the full editor with AdwNavigationView subpages, a reusable StringListGroup, and a debounced SpinRow. Make disabled agents editable, and show a reload/keep-mine banner when the file changes on disk. Do not port the old settings window just to throw it away.

Write a TestDBus harness that runs the real binary from a generated .service file. Validate it first against the Python provider, then require it to pass unchanged on Rust. Add installer snapshot and upgrade tests in a throwaway HOME with GSETTINGS_BACKEND=memory or keyfile.

Release on a pinned ubuntu-24.04 runner with gtk4 v4_14 / libadwaita v1_5, a glibc-symbol ceiling check (ldd/objdump <= 2.39), and a container smoke matrix (Fedora 43/44, Debian 13, Ubuntu 24.04/26.04, Arch, Tumbleweed) that runs --version plus the TestDBus provider test. Publish as a draft release with SHA256SUMS and an attestation.
Keep https gateways working: soup3 (GNOME-native, async on the main loop, a Cancellable for a sub-second timeout) or ureq with rustls. Don't ship a plain-HTTP-only client.
Keep a CI cross-readability check (Python tomllib plus config.load on every editor output) and TOML-1.0-only emission for as long as a Python rollback is supported.
Document per-distro source and prebuilt instructions, including rustup or trixie-backports for Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 13, and a toolbox build for Silverblue.
fatal_flaws: None of the plans relies on an API that the verified facts say does not exist. The flaws below are serious but not fatal.

Plan 3: one GTK-linked binary means a prebuilt install on a system missing libadwaita fails with a dynamic-loader error before the installer can print any hint. Every provider activation also pays for loading and resolving libgtk/libadwaita under BIND_NOW.
Plan 3: the default plain-HTTP ureq build rejects https:// gateway URLs that work with Python urllib today. That is a user-visible regression unless the rustls feature (or soup3) is chosen.

Plan 1: the end state keeps bash glue plus a permanent Python-generated Unicode table toolchain and a lookaround-based \w/\b emulation layer. This raises long-term maintenance cost and pushes \b patterns onto fancy-regex's backtracking engine.
Plan 1: rollback is guaranteed only through a schema freeze that lasts until 1.0, after 7 phases and multiple soaks. That delays any real extension of the editor and the config schema.
